approved: Sex Discrimination and Fair Work (Respect at Work) Amendment Bill 2021
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would strengthen protections against workplace sexual harassment by changing discrimination and employment laws.
It would adopt definitions from work health and safety laws to cover more types of workers, including interns and volunteers.
The time limit for the Australian Human Rights Commission to dismiss a complaint about harassment would be extended from 6 months to 24 months.
Clarify that sexual harassment based on sex is unlawful in more workplace situations.
Allow a single instance of sexual harassment to be stopped by the Fair Work Commission.
Give employees who have a miscarriage an entitlement to compassionate leave.
Make clear that sexual harassment can be a valid reason for dismissal.
Workers, employers, and the Australian Human Rights Commission and Fair Work Commission are affected.

Sex Discrimination and Fair Work (Respect at Work) Amendment Bill 2021 - Consideration in Detail - Implement the 55 recommendations

The government introduced the Sex Discrimination and Fair Work (Respect at Work) Amendment Bill 2021 to implement reforms from the Respect@Work report, including expanding sexual harassment protections to all workers, removing exemptions for public servants and parliamentarians, and extending the AHRC complaint termination period from six to 24 months. The bill also adds compassionate leave for miscarriage and clarifies that sexual harassment can be a valid reason for dismissal, with over $64 million allocated in the 2021–22 federal budget.

The speaker supported the Sex Discrimination and Fair Work (Respect at Work) Amendment Bill 2021, which implements recommendations from the Respect@Work report to strengthen legal frameworks against sexual harassment and expand coverage to judges, MPs, ministerial staff, state/territory public servants, volunteers, and interns.

The speaker argued the government's bill implements only six of the 55 Respect@Work report recommendations, omitting a positive duty on employers to prevent sexual harassment and explicit prohibition in the Fair Work Act. Labor supports expanding coverage to all workers, extending complaint timeframes, and adding sexual harassment as a valid dismissal reason, while moving amendments for substantive equality, a positive duty, explicit prohibition, union legal action, cost protections, and 10 days paid domestic violence leave.

The speaker commended the Sex Discrimination and Fair Work (Respect at Work) Amendment Bill 2021, arguing it will ensure women are treated equally and free from harassment in the workplace. He highlighted the bill’s provision extending two days of compassionate or bereavement leave to couples who suffer a miscarriage, noting over 70% of surveyed small businesses supported the change, and credited the Pink Elephants Support Network, naming co-founder Samantha Payne, COO Sarah-Jane Monahas, and board member Katrina Groshinski.

The Respect at Work Amendment Bill was condemned as a half-hearted response to the 55 recommendations of the Respect@Work report, with Labor set to pursue five Senate-rejected amendments: a positive duty on employers to prevent sexual harassment, an explicit prohibition in the Fair Work Act, substantive equality as an object of the Sex Discrimination Act, union representation for complainants, and cost protections. The Prime Minister was also criticised for failing to attend the March4Justice rally and for not releasing the Gaetjens report into his office’s knowledge of Brittany Higgins’s alleged sexual assault.

The speaker supported the Sex Discrimination and Fair Work (Respect at Work) Amendment Bill 2021, which introduces an equality of opportunity clause, clarifies sex-based harassment prohibitions, removes exemptions for state public servants and parliamentarians, extends the complaint time limit from six to 24 months, and adds compassionate leave for miscarriage. The bill implements several recommendations from the Respect@Work report, but the speaker argued that legislative change alone is insufficient and that cultural change is also needed.

The speaker argued the Sex Discrimination and Fair Work (Respect at Work) Amendment Bill 2021 fails to implement most of the 55 recommendations from Commissioner Kate Jenkins' Respect@Work report, accusing the government of ignoring the report for over a year and watering down the few recommendations it claims to adopt. The speaker stated a future Labor government would fully implement all 55 recommendations if the current government does not accept proposed amendments.

The Sex Discrimination and Fair Work (Respect at Work) Amendment Bill 2021 introduces new objects clauses for equality of opportunity, prohibits sex-based harassment, removes exemptions for state public servants, applies to MPs and judges, extends protections to all workers, and amends the Australian Human Rights Commission Act to allow 24-month investigations. The bill was supported, referencing the Respect@Work report and contributions from Elizabeth Broderick and Kate Jenkins.

The Morrison government introduced the Sex Discrimination and Fair Work (Respect at Work) Amendment Bill 2021, implementing legislative reforms from the Respect@Work report’s 55 recommendations, with over $64.3 million in funding for legal assistance and prevention initiatives. The speaker also criticised Labor for alleged hypocrisy on workplace safety, citing unreported sexual harassment and assault allegations against Labor MPs.

The independent MP argued the Sex Discrimination and Fair Work (Respect at Work) Amendment Bill 2021 is a missed opportunity, as the government has implemented only three of the 55 Respect@Work recommendations and rejected amendments to strengthen workplace protections. They criticised the government for delaying reforms and ignoring the call to fully implement the report.

The speaker argued the government has failed to implement all 55 recommendations of the Jenkins Respect@Work report, calling the bill a "half-baked effort" and a "shocking missed opportunity." They strongly endorsed Labor's amendments, criticised the Prime Minister for breaking his promise to Australian women, and highlighted the need for a positive duty on employers to prevent sexual harassment.

The speaker welcomed the Sex Discrimination and Fair Work (Respect at Work) Amendment Bill 2021 but argued it fails to implement all Respect@Work recommendations, criticising the added 'seriously' qualifier, the omission of positive duties on employers, and the lack of sex-based harassment protections in the Fair Work Act. The speaker also urged broader workplace definitions and action on cost orders as a barrier to justice.

The government argued that the Sex Discrimination and Fair Work (Respect at Work) Amendment Bill 2021 will streamline legal frameworks on workplace sexual harassment, expand prohibitions, and reduce procedural barriers for complainants, building on the *Roadmap for Respect* report.
